P8e: A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. Keep in mind that it's an outsider's view of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing them. Still, it's a powerful picture. She writes that they carry their babies with them and bring them into daily adult life. Children are around people of several ages and learn by taking part, and no one exhausted parent is expected to be a child's whole social world. While a nuclear household can recreate some of this, a real village can make it normal.

P2: I specifically brought up vaccination because it's one of the values I would have to share with a community if I was going to raise my kids there. I'm not trying to design a community for everyone. I just think some common ground around children's health would be required if parents are going to trust each other.
P3: The review from the kids, once they're grown, matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can talk forever about what they intended. The kids who lived through it might have something else to say.
P9: Experiments where kids don't sleep and live with their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and many loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.
P10: People should look directly at what's going on at Tamera's Children's Place instead of caricaturing it. Still, my biased opinion is that I prefer a system where kids are exposed to more people, but where their bond with their parents isn't made ideologically inconvenient.
P13: This could come out wrong, so the safeguards need to be spelled out. A children's territory can't be left unmonitored by adults, or become a place where older kids quietly lord it over younger ones, or where secrecy gets treated as independence.
P14: And I think it's a real problem that so many suburban folks treat any warm relationship between a kid and an adult who isn't related to them as suspicious. It's good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who notice when something changes, and who will act when something is wrong. That kind of fear can destroy the gift without actually preventing abuse.
P16: Give children real agency. They have the right to say "no," and no grownup has a right to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.
P17: Have a no-secrets rule. No grownup may ever make a child keep a secret from their mom or another adult the child trusts, whether it's a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. Even surprises have to have an ending date when they're told. Secrets meant to isolate the child are forbidden.
P18: Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Kids should know that their words have power, and that adults will listen to what they say and take it seriously. Don't interrogate them, or punish them if they aren't sure of everything, and don't let the teaching become a reason to dismiss what they report. A scared or confused kid may not tell the story perfectly and still need protecting.
P19: Hear the child even when they point a finger at someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Be clear about the process ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. Do whatever's needed right away to keep everyone safe, then make sure it's investigated competently and fairly, and that nobody's status buys silence.
P20: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, but a court sent them back after rejecting the state's blanket request. So state intervention can fail spectacularly, and closing a community off completely can fail too. Kids need more than one world.
P21: I also searched the research corpus for a single well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with a good record of the whole sequence: what they did, how it was assessed, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I failed to find one. It may be that cases came up but were handled in private, or sent somewhere else, but it means I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and anyone at risk all need access to competent help and review, outside the control of the home community.
P22: The Amish let their young people decide on their own whether to join the church once they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. Popular culture tends to blow Rumspringa out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.
P23: If the children never leave, the community can't know whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel, make friends, see other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
